title: How to Start an E-commerce Business in the UAE
summary: Learn how to start an e-commerce business in Dubai, from licences and legal requirements to payments, setup costs, and tips for growing your online store in the UAE.
body_markdown:
The UAE is making a strong case for anyone thinking about starting a business. In April 2026, the country ranked first globally in the[Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM) report](https://www.moet.gov.ae/en/-/uae-ranks-first-globally-in-the-gem-2025-2026-global-report-for-the-fifth-consecutive-year) for the fifth year in a row. More than one in five adults in the UAE is involved in entrepreneurship, according to the same report.


That tells you something about the opportunities here. And e-commerce is one way to tap into them.


But setting up an online store takes more than a good product and a website. You need the right business license, a plan for handling payments, and a clear understanding of the rules that apply to your business. Get the basics right, and you’ll have a much stronger foundation to grow from.


Here’s how to start an e-commerce business in Dubai, from choosing your setup to getting ready for your first sale.


## Why the UAE is a hotspot for E-commerce business entrepreneurs


The UAE offers more than a business-friendly reputation. A growing online shopping market, consumers who are comfortable buying on their phones, and a strong startup ecosystem give e-commerce founders some solid reasons to consider setting up here. Let’s look at the four major reasons:


- A fast-growing e-commerce market: The UAE’s e-commerce market reached[AED 42.2 billion](https://www.wam.ae/en/article/c2h35yn-uae-e-commerce-market-size-reaches-aed422-billion) in 2025, up from AED 17.6 billion in 2020. That’s a five-year compound annual growth rate of 19%, according to an EZDubai–Euromonitor International report.
- Digitally active consumers: The UAE ranked first globally for mobile online shopping in Visa’s 2025[Global Digital Shopping Index](https://www.visa.com/en-ae/newsroom/uae-mobile-shopping-digital-retail-insights) , with 37% of surveyed consumers shopping online through mobile devices. For new businesses, this makes a mobile-friendly store and checkout experience especially important.
- Government support for new businesses: The UAE ranked first globally in the 2025–2026[Global Entrepreneurship Monitor](https://www.moet.gov.ae/en/-/uae-ranks-first-globally-in-the-gem-2025-2026-global-report-for-the-fifth-consecutive-year) report for the fifth consecutive year. It also scored 7.0 on the National Entrepreneurial Context Index, which assesses how well a country supports entrepreneurship.
- Access to finance and growth opportunities: The UAE ranked second globally for entrepreneurial finance and ease of access to it in the same GEM report. For e-commerce founders, this points to a supportive funding environment, with financing options that can help businesses move beyond the launch stage.


## Legal requirements to start an e-commerce business in the UAE


Before you launch your online store, you need to get the legal basics right. The UAE has specific rules for online sellers, from business licensing and product approvals to customer data protection and tax registration. Here’s what you need to know.


### 1. Get the right e-commerce licence


You need a valid business licence that covers your intended e-commerce activities. You can generally choose between two routes:


Mainland licence Free zone licence


Issued by the relevant emirate's Department of Economic Development (DED) or equivalent authority. Issued by a free zone authority, such as Dubai CommerCity, EZDubai or RAKEZ.


Can be suitable if you plan to sell directly to customers across the UAE mainland. Can suit businesses targeting international markets or operating within a free zone.


Requirements and fees vary by emirate and business activity. Direct mainland sales may require additional approvals or an appropriate distribution arrangement.


Choose your setup based on where you intend to sell, what you plan to sell, and how you want to operate. Check the exact requirements with the relevant licensing authority before applying.


### 2. Comply with the UAE’s e-commerce law


[Federal Decree-Law No. 14](https://u.ae/en/information-and-services/business/Managing-and-growing-your-business/ecommerce) of 2023 on Modern Technology-Based Trade regulates online transactions through websites, apps, social media and digital marketplaces. As an online seller, you must:


- Sell only permitted goods and services and obtain any required product-specific approvals.
- Display accurate product descriptions, prices and terms. Avoid misleading claims.
- Issue a digital invoice for every transaction.
- Maintain secure technology systems and protect customer data in line with applicable privacy and cybersecurity requirements.


You may also need to comply with consumer protection rules and advertising regulations, especially if you promote products through social media.


### 3. Check additional approvals and permits


Depending on your business activity, you may need approvals from other authorities. For example, food, healthcare products and certain cosmetics may face additional regulatory requirements. The[UAE Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority (TDRA)](https://tdra.gov.ae/en/) also has a role in regulating digital trade. Confirm which approvals apply to your proposed activity with your licensing authority.


### 4. Understand your tax obligations


Register for[VAT with the Federal Tax Authority (FTA](https://tax.gov.ae/en/taxes/vat.aspx) ) if your taxable supplies and imports exceed the mandatory threshold of AED 375,000 over the relevant period. Voluntary registration is generally available from AED 187,500.


You should also assess whether your business must register for UAE corporate tax. The standard rate is 9% on taxable income exceeding AED 375,000, subject to applicable rules and exemptions. Free zone businesses should not automatically assume they are exempt from corporate tax.


## Step-by-step process to start an e-commerce business in the UAE


Getting an e-commerce business off the ground involves more than registering a domain and uploading product photos. Here’s how to approach the process without spending money on things you don’t need yet.


### 1. Validate demand before committing to a setup


Start with a specific customer and product category. Check what competitors charge on Amazon.ae and Noon, read customer reviews to spot unmet needs, and calculate your landed cost, including shipping, customs duties and packaging. If your margins only work when everything goes perfectly, revisit the product before investing in a licence or inventory.


### 2. Choose your business activity and jurisdiction


Decide whether you’ll sell physical products, digital goods or services. Then compare mainland and free zone licences based on your sales channels, warehouse needs and target markets.


Ask each licensing authority for an itemised quote covering registration, licence renewal, visas and any required approvals. A low first-year fee may not mean a low total operating cost.


### 3. Set up payments before building your store


Compare payment gateways based on transaction fees, settlement timelines, supported currencies and integration with your platform. If you expect international orders, check how the provider handles foreign cards, refunds, and chargebacks. Test the entire checkout process, including failed payments and refund notifications, before you launch.


### 4. Separate business finances from day one


Open a business account that matches your licence and operating needs. You’ll need it to receive sales revenue, pay suppliers, and track business expenses without mixing them with personal spending. An[AI-native Business Bank Account](https://www.alaan.com/business-banking) can help you manage business finances as your transactions grow. Also, budget for inventory, marketing, shipping, and refunds rather than treating all your available cash as money you can spend.


### 5. Launch small, then fix what doesn’t work


Start with a focused product range rather than a large catalogue. Before going live, test mobile checkout, payment confirmation, delivery estimates, customer support, and return instructions. Track three numbers during your first month: customer acquisition cost, gross margin per order, and the percentage of visitors who buy. These will tell you whether to invest in more inventory, improve your store, or rethink your marketing.


## E-commerce businesses in the UAE worth learning from


You don't have to look at global giants to understand what works in the UAE's e-commerce market. These businesses show how founders can build around a specific customer need, whether that's fresh groceries, underserved product categories or a more convenient way to shop.


### 1. Kibsons: Turning fresh produce into an online business


Kibsons started as a family-run fruit and vegetable business in Dubai in 1982. Under CEO Halima Jumani, it expanded into online grocery delivery, connecting its existing produce-sourcing expertise with growing demand for home delivery.


An October 2025[ACCA interview](https://abmagazine.accaglobal.com/global/articles/2025/oct/interviews/fresh-thinking.html) reported around 150,000 online orders a month and annual turnover of approximately US$100 million.


### 2. The Giving Movement: Turning a clear brand identity into an e-commerce business


Founded in Dubai in 2020 by entrepreneur Dominic Nowell-Barnes,[The Giving Movement](https://thegivingmovement.com/) built its online business around locally produced apparel, sustainability, and charitable giving. The brand[donates](https://www.imagesretailme.com/balancing-sustainability-and-profitability/) AED 15 from every sale to charity, giving customers a clear reason to connect with its mission beyond the products themselves.


### 3. Luved: Building a business around a frustrating problem


Founder Shaima Sibtain developed Luved after experiencing the friction involved in giving away her toddler's old clothes.[Launched in the UAE in 2026](https://www.imagesretailme.com/if-not-me-then-who-inside-luved-the-uaes-new-pre-loved-marketplace/?vs=297) , the marketplace brings buying, selling, and gifting second-hand goods into one digital platform.


## Final thoughts


Starting an e-commerce business in the UAE takes more than finding a product people want to buy. You need the right licence, a reliable payment setup, a plan for fulfilling orders, and a clear picture of your costs. Start small, test demand before committing to large inventory purchases, and keep an eye on your margins as sales grow. The UAE offers a supportive environment for entrepreneurs, but how you manage your business will determine how far you can take it.

## FAQs


1. How much does it cost to start an e-commerce business in Dubai?


The cost depends on your licence, business activity, jurisdiction, visa requirements, and operational needs. Mainland and free zone packages vary, so compare registration fees, renewals, payment processing, inventory, shipping, and marketing costs before deciding on a budget.


2. Do I need a licence to sell products online in the UAE?


Yes. You need a valid business licence that covers your e-commerce activities. You can apply through the relevant emirate's licensing authority or a free zone authority. Additional approvals may be required for regulated products or specific business activities.


3. Do e-commerce businesses in the UAE have to pay VAT?


E-commerce businesses must register for VAT if their taxable supplies and imports exceed the mandatory threshold of AED 375,000 over the relevant period. Voluntary registration is generally available from AED 187,500. Your VAT obligations depend on your business activities and applicable tax rules.


4. Can I run an e-commerce business in Dubai and sell internationally?


Yes. A UAE-registered e-commerce business can sell to international customers, subject to applicable licensing conditions and the laws of its target markets. You'll need to consider international payment processing, shipping costs, customs duties, product regulations, and cross-border tax obligations.
